content: Vietnamese coriander, scientifically known as Persicaria odorata (synonyms: Polygonum odoratum, family Polygonaceae), is a herb whose leaves are commonly utilized in Southeast Asian cuisine. It is also referred to in English as Vietnamese mint, Vietnamese cilantro, Cambodian mint, and hot mint. In Vietnam, it is called rau răm, while in Malaysia and Singapore, it is known as daun kesom or daun laksa (laksa leaf). In Thailand, it is referred to as pak pai (ผักไผ่). Despite its name, it is not botanically related to the mint family, though its general appearance and aroma are reminiscent of mint. This herb is particularly associated with Vietnamese cuisine, where it is often consumed fresh in dishes such as salads (including chicken salad) and raw summer rolls (gỏi cuốn). It is also used in soups like canh chua and stews such as fish kho tộ. Additionally, it is a popular accompaniment to hột vịt lộn (fertilized duck egg, known as balut in the Philippines). In Singapore and Malaysia, the shredded leaves are a key ingredient in laksa, a spicy soup, to the extent that the Malay name daun laksa translates to laksa leaf. In Australia, the plant is being studied as a potential source of essential oil, referred to as kesom oil. Characteristics Vietnamese coriander is a perennial plant that thrives in tropical and subtropical climates under warm and moist conditions. Under favorable circumstances, it can grow to a height of 15 to 30 cm. However, it may wither during winter or in excessively high temperatures. The upper surface of its leaves is dark green with chestnut-colored spots, while the underside is burgundy red. Its stem is segmented. In Vietnam, it can be cultivated or found growing wild. Components The essential oil of Vietnamese coriander contains aldehydes such as decanal (28%) and dodecanal (44%), as well as the alcohol decanol (11%). Sesquiterpenes, including α-humulene and β-caryophyllene, make up approximately 15% of its oil composition. Medicinal Uses According to Vietnamese experts, Vietnamese coriander has a bitter and spicy taste, is non-toxic, and possesses detoxifying properties. It is believed to be effective in treating conditions such as swelling, acne, indigestion, flatulence, and stomachaches. Effects on Health In traditional Vietnamese herbal medicine, Vietnamese coriander is used to suppress sexual urges. A Vietnamese saying, rau răm, giá sống (Vietnamese coriander, live bean sprouts), reflects the belief that Vietnamese coriander reduces sexual desire, while bean sprouts have the opposite effect. Many Buddhist monks cultivate Vietnamese coriander in their private gardens and consume it regularly as part of their celibate lifestyle.
